stem:
A 34-year-old woman is admitted by the medical team after her flatmate found her disorientated and feverish. She has been unusually aggressive for a day and has had two fits. MRI shows abnormal signal in the temporal lobes.

Which virus is the most important cause to consider?
why_correct: Herpes simplex virus is the commonest identified cause of sporadic viral encephalitis in the UK. It has a predilection for the temporal lobes, producing personality change, confusion and seizures. Intravenous aciclovir should be started immediately and CSF sent for HSV PCR. Source: NHS, Encephalitis, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Rotavirus causes gastroenteritis in young children. C. Respiratory syncytial virus causes bronchiolitis and respiratory infections, not temporal lobe encephalitis. D. Hepatitis A causes acute hepatitis. E. Norovirus causes vomiting and diarrhoea.
pearl: Temporal lobe involvement on MRI or EEG is a strong pointer towards herpes simplex encephalitis.
thinking: Fever and confusion ↓ Behavioural change and seizures ↓ Temporal lobe changes on MRI ↓ Commonest viral cause is HSV ↓ Start IV aciclovir
exam_trap: E, Norovirus — it is a very common virus that can cause febrile illness in adults, but it causes gastroenteritis, not brain infection.
takeaway: Herpes simplex virus is the key viral cause of encephalitis, especially with temporal lobe changes.

stem:
A 4-month-old boy who was born in another country is seen by the paediatric team. He failed his hearing tests, has a heart murmur from a patent ductus arteriosus and has bilateral cataracts. His mother remembers having a rash and swollen neck glands in the first weeks of pregnancy.

Which maternal infection is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Rubella in the first trimester can cross the placenta and cause congenital rubella syndrome. The classic features are sensorineural deafness, congenital heart disease such as patent ductus arteriosus, and eye defects including cataracts. The risk of defects is highest when infection occurs early in pregnancy. Source: UKHSA, Green Book chapter 28: Rubella, updated 2026.
why_wrong: A. Influenza does not cause this pattern of congenital defects. B. Hepatitis A is not associated with congenital malformations. C. A urinary infection does not cause congenital deafness or cataracts. D. Tonsillitis does not cross the placenta to cause fetal defects.
pearl: Rubella is prevented by MMR vaccination; MMR is a live vaccine, so it is not given during pregnancy and pregnancy should be avoided for one month afterwards.
thinking: Deafness ↓ Patent ductus arteriosus ↓ Cataracts ↓ Maternal rash early in pregnancy ↓ Congenital rubella syndrome
exam_trap: A, Influenza — a febrile illness in early pregnancy can seem relevant, but influenza does not cause the deafness, heart and eye triad.
takeaway: Sensorineural deafness, congenital heart disease and cataracts point to congenital rubella.

stem:
A 19-year-old university fresher sees the practice nurse. She is starting a new relationship and wants to avoid pregnancy, but she also wants to lower her chance of catching chlamydia or other infections.

Which method meets both aims?
why_correct: Barrier methods such as male and female condoms are the only contraceptives that also reduce the transmission of sexually transmitted infections. She can use condoms alone or alongside a more reliable hormonal or intrauterine method for extra pregnancy protection. Free condoms are available from sexual health services. Source: NICE CKS, Contraception - barrier methods and spermicides, 2026.
why_wrong: A. The progestogen-only pill prevents pregnancy but gives no STI protection. B. The copper IUD is highly effective contraception but does not protect against infection. C. The combined pill does not prevent STIs. E. The injection does not protect against STIs.
pearl: Using condoms together with a long-acting reversible method is sometimes called double Dutch and gives highly effective protection against both pregnancy and STIs.
thinking: Wants contraception ↓ Also wants infection protection ↓ Hormonal and intrauterine methods do not protect ↓ Barrier blocks fluid exchange ↓ Condoms
exam_trap: B, Copper intrauterine device — it is among the most effective contraceptives, which tempts, but it offers no protection against STIs.
takeaway: Condoms are the only contraceptive method that also protects against sexually transmitted infections.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman attends the infectious diseases clinic. She was found to have HIV two years ago but stopped antiretroviral therapy last year, and her CD4 count is now very low. Sputum culture has grown Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The registrar explains to the foundation doctor why this pairing of infections matters.

Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: Tuberculosis in people with HIV is usually confined to the lungs
options.B: Sputum smears are more likely to be positive as immunosuppression advances
options.C: HIV-related immunosuppression greatly increases progression from latent to active tuberculosis
options.D: Antiretroviral therapy should be withheld until the full course of tuberculosis treatment is finished
options.E: Contact tracing is unnecessary because co-infected patients cannot transmit tuberculosis

correct_answer: C. HIV-related immunosuppression greatly increases progression from latent to active tuberculosis
why_correct: Loss of CD4 cell-mediated immunity removes the main defence that keeps Mycobacterium tuberculosis contained in granulomas, so people with HIV are many times more likely to develop active disease, either from reactivation of latent infection or rapid progression of new infection. Disease is also more often extrapulmonary or disseminated. This is why everyone with tuberculosis should be offered an HIV test, and why co-infected patients need joint specialist care. Source: NICE NG33 Tuberculosis, 2016 (updated 2024).
why_wrong: A. Extrapulmonary and disseminated tuberculosis become more common, not less, as the CD4 count falls. B. Advanced HIV produces fewer cavities, so smear-negative disease is more frequent. D. Antiretroviral therapy is started during tuberculosis treatment rather than after it, earliest of all when the CD4 count is very low, because this improves survival. E. Pulmonary disease in co-infected patients can still be infectious, so contacts must be assessed.
pearl: Everyone diagnosed with active tuberculosis should be offered an HIV test, and everyone with newly diagnosed HIV should be assessed for tuberculosis.
thinking: HIV with very low CD4 count ↓ Cell-mediated immunity fails to contain mycobacteria ↓ Latent infection reactivates or new infection progresses quickly ↓ More active and extrapulmonary tuberculosis ↓ HIV greatly increases tuberculosis risk
exam_trap: D, Withholding antiretroviral therapy — concern about drug interactions and immune reconstitution makes delay seem sensible, but antiretrovirals are started during tuberculosis treatment because waiting increases mortality.
takeaway: HIV markedly increases the risk of developing active, often extrapulmonary, tuberculosis.

stem:
A mother phones NHS 111 in the evening. Since yesterday she, her husband and their two school-age children have all had sudden vomiting and loose watery stools. Nobody has blood in the stool, all are drinking, and none had bowel problems before this week.

Which diagnosis best explains the situation?
why_correct: Abrupt vomiting and watery stools affecting a whole family within a day or two points to a transmissible infection, most often viral, spread person to person or through shared food. Chronic bowel conditions develop over weeks to months in one individual and would not appear simultaneously in four people. Source: NICE CKS, Gastroenteritis, 2026.
why_wrong: B. Ulcerative colitis causes chronic bloody diarrhoea in one person, not a family cluster. C. Irritable bowel syndrome is a long-standing functional disorder and does not start suddenly in several relatives. D. Coeliac disease causes gradual symptoms after gluten exposure, not an acute shared illness. E. Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory condition with a subacute course.
pearl: Children with gastroenteritis should stay off school or nursery until 48 hours after the last episode of vomiting or diarrhoea.
thinking: Sudden onset ↓ Vomiting plus watery diarrhoea ↓ Several family members affected at once ↓ No prior bowel history ↓ Transmissible infective gastroenteritis
exam_trap: C, Irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea — it is a very common cause of loose stools, but it is chronic and cannot explain a sudden illness shared by a household.
takeaway: An acute cluster of vomiting and diarrhoea in one household is infective gastroenteritis until proven otherwise.

stem:
A 52-year-old man sees his GP with two days of fever, griping lower abdominal pain and frequent loose stools. Three days ago he ate a homemade dessert made with raw eggs at a family party, and his sister who ate the same dessert is also unwell.

Which bacterium is the most likely cause?
why_correct: Fever, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea starting a day or so after eating raw or undercooked egg is a classic picture of non-typhoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis. A second case linked to the same food supports a foodborne source. Most cases settle with fluids alone, and food poisoning is notifiable, so the local health protection team should be informed. Source: NHS, Food poisoning, 2024; UKHSA, Notifiable diseases and causative organisms, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Bordetella pertussis causes whooping cough, not foodborne diarrhoea. B. Treponema pallidum causes syphilis. D. Clostridium tetani causes tetanus with muscle spasm. E. Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease after a tick bite.
pearl: Antibiotics are not usually needed for non-typhoidal Salmonella and may prolong carriage; they are reserved for severe illness, the very young or old, and the immunocompromised.
thinking: Fever, cramps and diarrhoea ↓ Onset about a day after raw egg dessert ↓ Another person who ate it is unwell ↓ Foodborne bacterial gastroenteritis ↓ Salmonella
exam_trap: D, Clostridium tetani — the 'Clostridium' name suggests the diarrhoea-causing C. difficile, but C. tetani causes tetanus and has no role in food poisoning.
takeaway: Raw or undercooked egg followed by febrile diarrhoea suggests Salmonella.

stem:
A 70-year-old woman who was treated in hospital for Clostridioides difficile infection last winter asks her GP for antibiotics for a cough and sore throat that look viral. The GP advises against them and she asks how antibiotics led to her bowel infection.

Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: Antibiotics directly ulcerate the colonic lining, which then becomes secondarily infected
options.B: Antibiotics kill protective gut bacteria, letting C. difficile multiply and make toxins
options.C: Antibiotics trigger an allergic reaction in the colon that mimics infection
options.D: Antibiotics carry C. difficile spores into the bowel from the tablet coating
options.E: Antibiotics make C. difficile invade the bloodstream and seed the colon

correct_answer: B. Antibiotics kill protective gut bacteria, letting C. difficile multiply and make toxins
why_correct: The healthy colonic microbiota resists colonisation by C. difficile. Antibiotics, especially broad-spectrum agents, disrupt this flora, so ingested spores can germinate, multiply and release toxins A and B that damage the colon. Avoiding antibiotics that are not needed is therefore a key part of preventing first and recurrent episodes. Source: NICE NG199 Clostridioides difficile infection: antimicrobial prescribing, 2021; NICE CKS, Diarrhoea - antibiotic associated, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Antibiotics do not ulcerate the colon directly; the damage comes from C. difficile toxins. C. The colitis is toxin-mediated infection, not an allergic reaction. D. Spores are acquired from the environment or contacts, not from medicines. E. C. difficile is a non-invasive luminal pathogen and does not spread through the blood.
pearl: Clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav and fluoroquinolones carry the highest risk, and proton pump inhibitors add to it.
thinking: Previous C. difficile infection ↓ Antibiotics disturb protective gut flora ↓ Spores germinate and multiply ↓ Toxins injure the colon ↓ Avoid unnecessary antibiotics to prevent recurrence
exam_trap: A, Direct ulceration by antibiotics — it sounds like a plausible drug side effect, but the injury comes from bacterial toxins after the protective flora is lost.
takeaway: Antibiotics cause C. difficile infection by wiping out the normal flora that keeps it in check.

stem:
Over two weeks, several children and parents who used the same leisure centre swimming pool present to local GPs with watery, non-bloody diarrhoea and stomach cramps. A 34-year-old father among them has had symptoms for nine days. UKHSA notes that the parasite involved is resistant to routine pool chlorination.

Which protozoan is most likely?
why_correct: Cryptosporidium is a protozoan whose oocysts resist chlorine, so it is the classic cause of outbreaks linked to swimming pools and water supplies. It causes watery diarrhoea and cramps that usually settle within a couple of weeks in immunocompetent people. Diagnosis is by stool testing (antigen, PCR or microscopy) for Cryptosporidium, and linked cases are investigated by the local health protection team. Source: Public Health Agency Northern Ireland, Cryptosporidium factsheet, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery with bloody stools, usually acquired abroad. B. Plasmodium falciparum causes malaria, transmitted by mosquitoes. C. Toxoplasma gondii is acquired from cat faeces or undercooked meat and usually causes a glandular fever-like illness or congenital infection. E. Trichomonas vaginalis is a sexually transmitted protozoan causing vaginal discharge.
pearl: In people with advanced HIV, cryptosporidiosis can cause chronic, severe watery diarrhoea and wasting.
thinking: Cluster linked to one swimming pool ↓ Watery, non-bloody diarrhoea with cramps ↓ Organism survives chlorination ↓ Protozoan with resistant oocysts ↓ Cryptosporidium
exam_trap: A, Entamoeba histolytica — it is the best-known gut protozoan, but it causes bloody dysentery and is not the typical chlorine-resistant pool outbreak organism.
takeaway: Watery diarrhoea outbreaks linked to swimming pools are classically due to Cryptosporidium.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct: replaced unsupported claim that Cryptosporidium testing must be specially requested with neutral diagnosis/health protection statement

stem:
Twenty pupils and two teachers fall ill with vomiting and watery diarrhoea during a school camping trip. The toilet block had no soap, and the same tap was used for drinking and washing up. The environmental health officer asks the visiting doctor how the infection most likely spread.

Which route is most likely?
why_correct: Outbreaks of vomiting and diarrhoea are usually caused by organisms passed from faeces to the mouth through contaminated hands, food or water. Missing soap and a shared tap for drinking and washing up provide exactly these routes. Hand hygiene with soap and water and safe food and water handling are the key control measures. Source: NICE CKS, Gastroenteritis, 2026.
why_wrong: A. Insect vectors transmit infections such as malaria and dengue, not acute gastroenteritis outbreaks. B. Blood-borne spread applies to hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV. C. Sexual transmission does not explain a sudden group outbreak in a school party. D. Vertical spread occurs from mother to baby in pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding.
pearl: Hepatitis A and typhoid are also spread by the faeco-oral route; food handlers with gastroenteritis should stay off work until 48 hours after their symptoms have stopped.
thinking: Group outbreak of vomiting and diarrhoea ↓ No soap at the toilets ↓ Shared tap for drinking and washing up ↓ Contaminated hands, food and water ↓ Faeco-oral transmission
exam_trap: A, Mosquito-borne spread — camping outdoors makes insect bites seem relevant, but mosquitoes do not cause outbreaks of acute vomiting and diarrhoea.
takeaway: Outbreaks of gastroenteritis are usually spread by the faeco-oral route.
notes: Reviewer fix: pearl: reworded muddled link between hepatitis A/typhoid and the 48-hour food-handler exclusion

stem:
A 58-year-old man who moved to the UK from Pakistan two years ago is admitted with a month of night sweats, drenching fevers and marked weight loss. He takes methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis. His chest X-ray shows countless tiny nodules scattered evenly through both lungs, liver enzymes are raised and fundoscopy reveals small pale choroidal lesions.

Which form of disease best accounts for this picture?
why_correct: Miliary tuberculosis results from haematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, seeding many organs at once. The diffuse 'millet seed' nodules on chest X-ray, abnormal liver tests and choroidal tubercles in an immunosuppressed man from a high-incidence country fit dissemination rather than localised lung disease. It is a medical emergency needing prompt specialist treatment. Source: NICE NG33 Tuberculosis, 2016 (updated 2024).
why_wrong: A. Latent infection is asymptomatic and does not cause fever, weight loss or radiological lesions. B. Metastases are usually fewer, larger and of variable size, and would not explain choroidal tubercles. C. Sarcoidosis typically causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and is less likely with drenching fevers in this setting. D. Post-primary disease usually causes upper lobe cavitation rather than uniform tiny nodules in several organs.
pearl: Choroidal tubercles on fundoscopy are highly specific for miliary tuberculosis and can support the diagnosis before cultures return.
thinking: Immunosuppressed man from a high-incidence country ↓ Systemic symptoms with weight loss ↓ Uniform tiny nodules throughout both lungs ↓ Liver and eye involvement suggest blood-borne spread ↓ Disseminated (miliary) tuberculosis
exam_trap: D, Cavitating post-primary tuberculosis — it is the commonest active form in adults, but cavitation is localised to the upper lobes and does not explain multi-organ seeding.
takeaway: Diffuse tiny lung nodules with involvement of other organs indicates haematogenous, miliary spread of tuberculosis.

stem:
In late summer, a 47-year-old forestry worker from the Scottish Highlands sees his GP because the left side of his face has drooped over the past day and he cannot close his left eye. About six weeks earlier he noticed a spreading red ring on his calf that faded on its own, and he has since had aching joints and fatigue. His forehead is also weak on the affected side.

Which infection is the most likely underlying cause?
why_correct: Lyme disease, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi from tick bites, can cause neurological involvement weeks after the initial rash, and facial nerve palsy is the commonest cranial neuropathy. An outdoor worker in a tick area with a previous expanding ring-shaped rash, arthralgia and lower motor neurone facial weakness fits early disseminated Lyme disease. Source: NICE NG95 Lyme disease, 2018.
why_wrong: B. Herpes simplex type 2 causes genital lesions and occasionally meningitis, not this tick-linked picture. C. Tetanus causes muscle rigidity and spasms such as trismus, not flaccid facial palsy. D. Influenza does not typically cause an isolated facial nerve palsy weeks after a rash. E. Hepatitis A causes an acute hepatitis rather than cranial nerve palsy.
pearl: Facial palsy in Lyme disease can be bilateral, which is rare in idiopathic Bell's palsy and should prompt consideration of Lyme disease.
thinking: Outdoor worker in a tick-endemic area ↓ Previous expanding ring-shaped rash that faded ↓ Arthralgia and fatigue since ↓ Lower motor neurone facial palsy weeks later ↓ Early disseminated Lyme disease
exam_trap: B, Herpes simplex type 2 infection — herpes viruses are linked with facial palsy, but the preceding expanding rash and tick exposure point to Borrelia.
takeaway: Facial nerve palsy weeks after a tick bite or erythema migrans should prompt testing and treatment for Lyme disease.

stem:
A foundation doctor on a surgical ward is asked to take blood cultures from a 66-year-old man with rigors two days after a bowel resection. A senior nurse reminds her to clean the skin with chlorhexidine in alcohol, let it dry, avoid touching the site again and disinfect the bottle tops before inoculating them.

What is the main purpose of this careful technique?

options.A: To stop skin organisms entering the bloodstream and causing bacteraemia
options.B: To allow the samples to be taken after antibiotics have started
options.C: To avoid contaminating the sample and producing false-positive results
options.D: To improve the detection of fungal infection
options.E: To reduce the volume of blood needed in each bottle

correct_answer: C. To avoid contaminating the sample and producing false-positive results
why_correct: Skin commensals such as coagulase-negative staphylococci can easily enter the bottles if technique is poor, giving false-positive cultures. Contaminated results lead to unnecessary antibiotics, extra tests, longer stays and confusion about the true cause of sepsis, so aseptic non-touch technique protects the accuracy of the result. Source: UK Standards for Microbiology Investigations B 37, Investigation of blood cultures, UKHSA, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Venepuncture rarely causes bacteraemia; the purpose of asepsis is the integrity of the sample. B. Cultures should ideally be taken before antibiotics whatever technique is used. D. Aseptic technique does not specifically improve fungal yield. E. Adequate filling of each bottle is still needed, as volume is a major factor in sensitivity.
pearl: The volume of blood cultured is one of the most important factors in sensitivity; underfilled bottles miss genuine bacteraemia.
thinking: Febrile post-operative patient needs cultures ↓ Skin flora can enter the sample ↓ Contaminants grow and look like true pathogens ↓ False positives drive unnecessary treatment ↓ Asepsis is about sample accuracy
exam_trap: A, Preventing bacteraemia — asepsis sounds like it protects the patient from infection, but its purpose in blood culture collection is to prevent contamination of the sample.
takeaway: Aseptic technique for blood cultures prevents contamination and misleading false-positive results.

stem:
A 31-year-old man is seen in a medical admissions unit with two days of fever, extreme anxiety and episodes of throat spasm when he tries to drink water. Seven weeks ago, while volunteering in rural India, he was bitten on the hand by a stray dog and did not seek treatment. He now becomes agitated when a fan blows air at his face.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Rabies is a lyssavirus infection transmitted by bites from infected mammals, particularly dogs in endemic regions. After an incubation of weeks to months it causes encephalitis with agitation, hydrophobia and aerophobia from pharyngeal spasm. Once symptoms appear it is almost always fatal, so post-exposure prophylaxis after any potential exposure is vital. Source: UKHSA, Rabies: epidemiology, transmission and prevention, 2025; UKHSA, Rabies risk assessment, post-exposure treatment and management, 2026.
why_wrong: A. Tetanus causes trismus and muscle rigidity but not hydrophobia or aerophobia. B. Botulism causes descending flaccid paralysis with clear consciousness. D. Viral meningitis causes headache and neck stiffness without throat spasm on drinking. E. Lyme disease follows tick bites and causes rash, arthralgia or cranial nerve palsy.
pearl: Any bite or scratch from a potentially rabid animal abroad needs prompt wound washing and urgent post-exposure assessment following UKHSA guidance, even weeks later.
thinking: Dog bite in a rabies-endemic country ↓ No post-exposure prophylaxis ↓ Weeks of incubation ↓ Agitation with spasm on drinking or air on the face ↓ Rabies encephalitis
exam_trap: A, Tetanus — it also follows wounds and causes spasms, but hydrophobia and aerophobia are characteristic of rabies.
takeaway: Hydrophobia and agitation weeks after an animal bite abroad suggest rabies.

stem:
Two weeks after returning from a holiday in the Caribbean, a 38-year-old man sees his GP with five days of fever, a widespread itchy red rash and severe pain and swelling in his wrists, fingers and ankles on both sides. He recalls many mosquito bites. He has had no diarrhoea, urethral discharge or new sexual partners, and no joint is hot and red.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Fever, rash and acute symmetrical polyarthritis of the small joints after many mosquito bites in the Caribbean is typical of chikungunya, an alphavirus spread by Aedes mosquitoes. Joint pain can be severe and may persist for weeks to months. Dengue and Zika can look similar, and malaria should still be excluded when travel has been to an endemic area. Source: UKHSA, Chikungunya guidance, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Disseminated gonococcal infection causes tenosynovitis, a sparse pustular rash and arthritis after a recent sexual exposure, which he denies. C. Reactive arthritis follows gut or genital infection and is usually an asymmetrical large-joint oligoarthritis. D. Gout rarely starts in several small joints at once and does not cause a widespread rash with fever. E. Rheumatoid arthritis develops more gradually and is not accompanied by an acute febrile rash.
pearl: Chikungunya means 'that which bends up', describing the stooped posture caused by severe joint pain, which can persist for months.
thinking: Recent Caribbean travel with mosquito bites  ↓  Fever and widespread rash  ↓  Acute symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis  ↓  No gut, genital or sexual trigger  ↓  Chikungunya
exam_trap: C, Post-infective reactive arthritis — joint symptoms after travel suggest it, but there was no preceding diarrhoea or genital infection and the pattern is symmetrical small-joint disease with a rash.
takeaway: Fever, rash and polyarthritis after tropical travel suggests a viral cause such as chikungunya.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman attends her GP with five days of high temperatures, a painful throat, mouth ulcers and a faint blotchy rash over her trunk. She has tender nodes in the neck, axillae and groins. Three weeks ago she had condomless sex with a new partner she met abroad. A glandular fever screen is negative.

Which condition is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: A flu-like or glandular-fever-like illness with rash, mouth ulcers and generalised lymphadenopathy two to four weeks after a sexual exposure is the typical picture of HIV seroconversion. A negative glandular fever screen makes EBV less likely. She should be offered a fourth-generation HIV test (antigen and antibody), which detects infection early; viral load is very high at this stage, so early diagnosis also reduces onward transmission. Source: NICE CKS, HIV infection and AIDS, 2025; BHIVA, UK guidelines for HIV testing, 2020.
why_wrong: A. Glandular fever is the main mimic, but the screen is negative and mouth ulcers with a truncal rash after a recent sexual exposure point to HIV. B. Streptococcal tonsillitis does not cause generalised lymphadenopathy with a rash and mucosal ulcers. C. Hodgkin lymphoma causes painless nodes developing over weeks to months, not an acute febrile illness. E. Sarcoidosis causes hilar nodes, erythema nodosum and arthralgia rather than a seroconversion illness.
pearl: BHIVA advises HIV testing in anyone with a glandular-fever-like illness, as primary HIV infection is frequently missed at first presentation.
thinking: Acute febrile illness with sore throat, mouth ulcers and rash ↓ Generalised lymphadenopathy ↓ Condomless sex with a new partner three weeks earlier ↓ Glandular fever screen negative ↓ Seroconversion illness: offer fourth-generation HIV test
exam_trap: A, Infectious mononucleosis — the sore throat and widespread nodes look like glandular fever, but a negative screen and recent sexual exposure should prompt an HIV test.
takeaway: Think of primary HIV infection in any glandular-fever-like illness after a recent sexual exposure, and test for it.

stem:
A 63-year-old man is brought to the ED by his wife because he has become confused and drowsy over the course of the day. He has been treated for a painful left ear for a week. He is febrile, resists neck flexion and has no rash. After blood cultures and antibiotics, a lumbar puncture is done and the CSF Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci.

Which organism is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest cause of bacterial meningitis in adults in the UK. Spread from a contiguous focus such as otitis media is a classic route, and pneumococci appear as Gram-positive diplococci on CSF microscopy. Pneumococcal meningitis carries a high mortality and risk of hearing loss, which is why dexamethasone is given alongside antibiotics. Source: NICE NG240 Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Listeria affects older or immunocompromised adults but appears as Gram-positive rods, not diplococci. B. Meningococci are Gram-negative diplococci and are more typical in younger people, often with a purpuric rash. D. Staphylococcus epidermidis causes shunt or device infections rather than community-acquired meningitis. E. Cryptococcus causes subacute meningitis in immunocompromised people and is seen on India ink staining, not as diplococci.
pearl: Recent otitis media, sinusitis, skull fracture with CSF leak, alcohol excess or splenectomy all raise the likelihood of pneumococcal meningitis.
thinking: Fever, confusion and neck stiffness in an older adult ↓ Preceding ear infection as a source ↓ CSF shows Gram-positive diplococci ↓ Commonest adult cause of bacterial meningitis ↓ Streptococcus pneumoniae
exam_trap: B, Neisseria meningitidis — meningococcus is the best-known cause of meningitis, but it is a Gram-negative diplococcus and the ear source points to pneumococcus.
takeaway: In adults, especially with an ear or sinus source, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the leading cause of bacterial meningitis.

stem:
At an urgent treatment centre, a 30-year-old woman who missed her childhood immunisations is seen with four days of fever, a runny nose, a hacking cough and sore red eyes. Today a blotchy red rash appeared at her hairline and is spreading down her body. Small white spots are seen on the inside of her cheeks.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Return her to the shared waiting area wearing a surgical face mask
options.B: Keep her in the waiting room until her measles test result returns
options.C: Move her promptly to a single room away from other patients
options.D: Start oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for presumed scarlet fever
options.E: Give a dose of MMR vaccine now to shorten the illness

correct_answer: C. Move her promptly to a single room away from other patients
why_correct: A prodrome of fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis followed by a rash spreading down from the hairline, with Koplik spots, makes measles very likely in this unimmunised adult. Measles spreads by the airborne route and is extremely infectious, so the immediate priority is to move her out of shared areas into a single room with the door closed. Staff should then notify the local health protection team on clinical suspicion and arrange testing, without waiting for confirmation. Source: UKHSA, National measles guidelines version 8, 2026.
why_wrong: A. A surgical mask does not make it safe for someone with an airborne infection such as measles to share a waiting area with vulnerable patients. B. Waiting for a result before isolating her exposes others, including pregnant women and infants, while she is highly infectious. D. Cough, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots point to measles rather than scarlet fever, so antibiotics are not indicated. E. MMR given to someone already ill with measles does not change the course; post-exposure MMR is for susceptible contacts.
pearl: Measles is infectious from about four days before to four days after the onset of the rash, and susceptible contacts may need post-exposure MMR or immunoglobulin.
thinking: Unimmunised adult  ↓  Fever with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis  ↓  Rash spreading down from the hairline with Koplik spots  ↓  Measles is airborne and highly infectious  ↓  Isolate in a single room now, then notify
exam_trap: A, A mask in the waiting area — masks help with droplet infections, but measles is airborne and she needs a single room away from others.
takeaway: Suspected measles needs immediate airborne isolation and notification on clinical grounds, without waiting for results.

stem:
A GP reviews a 39-year-old man with a high temperature, sweats and headache for two days. He works for an engineering firm and has made several work trips overseas this year, some of them to tropical countries. The GP is considering malaria.

Which part of the history is most important to establish?

options.A: The airline and class of seat he flew in
options.B: Whether he has valid travel insurance
options.C: Exactly where and when he travelled
options.D: The brand of sun cream he used
options.E: Whether he ate any spicy food abroad

correct_answer: C. Exactly where and when he travelled
why_correct: Malaria risk depends on where someone has been, including rural or urban areas within a country, and when. Knowing exact destinations confirms whether he entered an endemic area, and the dates show whether the timing fits the incubation period; falciparum usually presents within weeks, while vivax and ovale can relapse months later. This history guides the urgency of blood films and specialist advice. Source: UKHSA, Malaria prevention guidelines for travellers from the UK, 2026.
why_wrong: A. The airline and seat class have no bearing on malaria exposure. B. Insurance may matter practically but does not affect the clinical risk assessment. D. Sun cream does not protect against mosquito bites or affect risk. E. Spicy food has no relevance to malaria.
pearl: Also ask about antimalarial prophylaxis and adherence, bite avoidance, and stopovers, but prophylaxis never excludes malaria.
thinking: Fever after several overseas trips ↓ Malaria risk varies by region and season ↓ Destination confirms exposure ↓ Dates check fit with the incubation period ↓ Establish exact places and dates of travel
exam_trap: E, Spicy food — dietary history feels relevant to illness abroad, but food has nothing to do with malaria risk, which depends on where and when he travelled.
takeaway: In fever after travel, record exactly where the person went and when.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman calls her GP surgery two days after returning from a backpacking trip in South-East Asia, where there has been an outbreak of dengue. She has a high temperature, pain behind her eyes and severe muscle and joint aches, and she asks what she can take from her medicine cabinet.

Which medicine should she be advised not to take?
why_correct: Dengue can cause thrombocytopenia and, in severe forms, plasma leakage and bleeding. Aspirin and other NSAIDs impair platelet function and increase the risk of haemorrhage, so they should be avoided until dengue has been excluded. Paracetamol at standard doses and good oral hydration are the mainstays of symptom relief, with medical review for warning signs such as abdominal pain, persistent vomiting or bleeding. Source: nidirect (NHS information, Northern Ireland), Dengue, accessed 2026; UKHSA, Dengue fever guidance, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Paracetamol is the recommended analgesic and antipyretic in suspected dengue. B. Oral rehydration supports fluid balance and is encouraged. D. Cetirizine does not affect platelets and is safe for itch. E. Ondansetron can be used for nausea and does not increase bleeding risk.
pearl: Warning signs of severe dengue often appear as the fever settles, around days three to seven, so worsening at defervescence should prompt urgent review.
thinking: Fever, retro-orbital pain and myalgia after travel to an endemic area ↓ Suspected dengue ↓ Risk of low platelets and bleeding ↓ Aspirin and NSAIDs worsen bleeding risk ↓ Avoid aspirin; use paracetamol
exam_trap: A, Paracetamol — some think all medicines should be withheld in a returning traveller, but paracetamol is the preferred option and it is aspirin that must be avoided.
takeaway: In suspected dengue, avoid aspirin and NSAIDs and use paracetamol for symptom relief.

stem:
After a wedding reception, about a dozen guests develop abrupt vomiting and stomach cramps between two and four hours after eating from a cold buffet of ham sandwiches and cream cakes. Nobody has a fever and most feel better by the next morning. One of the caterers had an infected cut on her hand.

Which organism is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Staphylococcus aureus from an infected skin lesion on a food handler can contaminate food, multiply at room temperature and produce a heat-stable preformed enterotoxin. Because the toxin is already present, vomiting begins within a few hours of eating and settles within about a day without fever. Cold meats, sandwiches and cream products are typical vehicles. Source: UKHSA, Notifiable diseases and causative organisms, 2025; NHS, Food poisoning, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Campylobacter has an incubation of several days and causes fever and often bloody diarrhoea. B. Salmonella usually starts 12 to 72 hours after eating, with fever and diarrhoea. C. Clostridium perfringens typically causes diarrhoea and cramps 8 to 16 hours after reheated meat dishes, with little vomiting. D. Escherichia coli O157 has an incubation of several days and causes bloody diarrhoea with a risk of haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
pearl: Food poisoning is notifiable in the UK, and suspected outbreaks should be reported to the local health protection team.
thinking: Group outbreak after a shared meal ↓ Vomiting within a few hours, no fever ↓ Short course, settling within a day ↓ Food handler with an infected skin lesion ↓ Preformed toxin of Staphylococcus aureus
exam_trap: C, Clostridium perfringens — it is a classic outbreak organism after catered meals, but its onset is later and diarrhoea, not vomiting, predominates.
takeaway: Vomiting within a few hours of eating, without fever, points to a preformed toxin such as staphylococcal enterotoxin.
notes: Reviewer fix: Option B serovar capitalised (Salmonella Enteritidis).

stem:
A family of four calls NHS 111 because all of them started vomiting within two hours of eating egg fried rice. The rice had been cooked the day before, left on the kitchen worktop overnight and then briefly reheated in a wok. None of them has a fever.

Which organism is most likely responsible?
why_correct: Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking of rice and germinate if the rice is left at room temperature, producing a heat-stable emetic toxin. Brief reheating does not destroy the toxin, so vomiting starts within one to five hours of eating and usually resolves within a day. Cooked rice should be cooled quickly and refrigerated. Source: Food Standards Scotland, Rice: storing and reheating safely, accessed 2026.
why_wrong: A. Campylobacter has an incubation of two to five days and causes fever with diarrhoea. B. Clostridium perfringens causes diarrhoea rather than vomiting, usually 8 to 16 hours after meat dishes. C. Listeria causes a febrile illness or invasive disease after days to weeks and is linked to chilled foods. D. Norovirus has an incubation of 12 to 48 hours and spreads person to person rather than from one reheated dish.
pearl: Bacillus cereus has two syndromes: a rapid emetic illness from preformed toxin (rice) and a later diarrhoeal illness from toxin produced in the gut.
thinking: Whole household affected after one dish ↓ Vomiting within two hours ↓ Cooked rice stored at room temperature and reheated ↓ Heat-stable emetic toxin ↓ Bacillus cereus
exam_trap: D, Norovirus — it causes outbreaks of vomiting in households, but its incubation is a day or more, not two hours after a single meal.
takeaway: Rapid vomiting after reheated rice is classically due to Bacillus cereus toxin.

stem:
A 22-year-old man books a sexual health appointment because his new partner noticed bumps on his penis. On examination there are one to two rows of tiny, smooth, dome-shaped, skin-coloured papules evenly spaced around the corona of the glans. They are not itchy or painful, and he thinks they have been there for years.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Pearly penile papules are a common normal anatomical variant: small, uniform, dome-shaped papules arranged in rows around the corona. They are not infectious, not sexually transmitted and need no treatment. The main task is to recognise them and reassure the patient so that unnecessary treatment for warts is avoided. Source: Primary Care Dermatology Society, Pearly penile papules, 2021.
why_wrong: A. Warts are irregular, often cauliflower-like and scattered rather than in neat symmetrical rows on the corona. B. Molluscum lesions are pearly but umbilicated and scattered, not uniformly arranged. C. Fordyce spots are tiny yellow-white sebaceous glands, typically on the shaft or scrotum. D. Lichen planus causes violaceous papules or annular lesions, often itchy, with Wickham striae.
pearl: Pearly penile papules do not respond to wart treatments, and applying them can cause irritation without benefit.
thinking: Asymptomatic papules present for years ↓ Uniform, dome-shaped, skin-coloured ↓ Arranged in rows around the corona ↓ Normal variant, not an infection ↓ Pearly penile papules: reassure
exam_trap: A, Anogenital warts — any penile papule raises concern about HPV, but warts are irregular and scattered rather than in symmetrical rows on the corona.
takeaway: Neat rows of tiny dome-shaped papules on the corona are pearly penile papules, a harmless normal variant.

presentation: Painless genital ulcer: referral for syphilis testing
stem:
A 44-year-old man sees his GP about a sore in the groove just behind the head of his penis, which he noticed about a week ago. It is a single ulcer with a clean base and a firm, rubbery edge, and it does not hurt. He has had several new male partners over the past three months.

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Prescribe topical clotrimazole and review in two weeks
options.B: Start oral aciclovir and review if not healing
options.C: Refer routinely to dermatology for a biopsy
options.D: Refer urgently to sexual health for syphilis testing
options.E: Apply a mild topical steroid and review in a month

correct_answer: D. Refer urgently to sexual health for syphilis testing
why_correct: A single painless indurated ulcer after recent new partners is a primary syphilitic chancre until proven otherwise. A sexual health service can test the lesion directly (dark-ground microscopy or PCR), send serology, screen for other infections including HIV, treat with benzathine penicillin and arrange partner notification. Prompt referral matters because the chancre heals on its own while the infection progresses. Source: NICE CKS, Syphilis, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Clotrimazole treats candida, which does not cause a painless ulcer, and delays diagnosis. B. Herpes ulcers are usually painful and multiple, and empirical aciclovir without testing would miss syphilis. C. A routine dermatology biopsy causes delay and misses the sexual health work-up and partner notification. E. A topical steroid has no role in an undiagnosed ulcer and may mask the diagnosis.
pearl: Do not apply topical antiseptics or antibiotics to a suspected chancre before swabbing, as they reduce the chance of detecting treponemes.
thinking: Single painless indurated penile ulcer ↓ Recent new sexual partners ↓ Suspected primary syphilis ↓ Needs lesion testing, serology, STI screen and partner notification ↓ Refer to a sexual health clinic
exam_trap: B, Oral aciclovir — genital ulcers are often assumed to be herpes, but herpes is painful and this painless indurated ulcer needs syphilis testing.
takeaway: A painless genital ulcer needs prompt sexual health assessment for syphilis, not empirical treatment.
